passage.sceneTitle: The New Neighbour Comes to the Assembly
passage.preamble: A rich young man called Mr Bingley has taken the big house near the Bennet family. Mrs Bennet has five grown-up daughters, and everyone in the village is waiting to see him at the next dance.

numberedLines.text: “If I can but see one of my daughters happily settled at Netherfield,” said Mrs. Bennet
to her husband, “and all the others equally well married, I shall have nothing to wish
for.”
In a few days Mr. Bingley returned Mr. Bennet’s visit, and sat about ten minutes with
him in his library. He had entertained hopes of being admitted to a sight of the young
ladies, of whose beauty he had heard much; but he saw only the father. The ladies were
somewhat more fortunate, for they had the advantage of ascertaining, from an upper
window, that he wore a blue coat and rode a black horse.
An invitation to dinner was soon afterwards despatched; and already had Mrs. Bennet
planned the courses that were to do credit to her housekeeping, when an answer arrived
which deferred it all. Mr. Bingley was obliged to be in town the following day, and
consequently unable to accept the honour of their invitation, etc. Mrs. Bennet was quite
disconcerted. She could not imagine what business he could have in town so soon after
his arrival in Hertfordshire; and she began to fear that he might always be flying about
from one place to another, and never settled at Netherfield as he ought to be. Lady
Lucas quieted her fears a little by starting the idea of his being gone to London only
to get a large party for the ball; and a report soon followed that Mr. Bingley was to
bring twelve ladies and seven gentlemen with him to the assembly. The girls grieved over
such a number of ladies; but were comforted the day before the ball by hearing that,
instead of twelve, he had brought only six with him from London, his five sisters and a
cousin. And when the party entered the assembly-room, it consisted of only five
altogether: Mr. Bingley, his two sisters, the husband of the eldest, and another young
man.
Mr. Bingley was good-looking and gentlemanlike: he had a pleasant countenance, and easy,
unaffected manners. His sisters were fine women, with an air of decided fashion. His
brother-in-law, Mr. Hurst, merely looked the gentleman; but his friend Mr. Darcy soon
drew the attention of the room by his fine, tall person, handsome features, noble mien,
and the report, which was in general circulation within five minutes after his entrance,
of his having ten thousand a year. The gentlemen pronounced him to be a fine figure of a
man, the ladies declared he was much handsomer than Mr. Bingley, and he was looked at
with great admiration for about half the evening, till his manners gave a disgust which
turned the tide of his popularity; for he was discovered to be proud, to be above his
company, and above being pleased; and not all his large estate in Derbyshire could save
him from having a most forbidding, disagreeable countenance, and being unworthy to be
compared with his friend.
Mr. Bingley had soon made himself acquainted with all the principal people in the room:
he was lively and unreserved, danced every dance, was angry that the ball closed so
early, and talked of giving one himself at Netherfield. Such amiable qualities must
speak for themselves. What a contrast between him and his friend! Mr. Darcy danced only
once with Mrs. Hurst and once with Miss Bingley, declined being introduced to any other
lady, and spent the rest of the evening in walking about the room, speaking occasionally
to one of his own party. His character was decided. He was the proudest, most
disagreeable man in the world, and everybody hoped that he would never come there again.
Amongst the most violent against him was Mrs. Bennet, whose dislike of his general
behaviour was sharpened into particular resentment by his having slighted one of her
daughters.
Elizabeth Bennet had been obliged, by the scarcity of gentlemen, to sit down for two
dances; and during part of that time, Mr. Darcy had been standing near enough for her to
overhear a conversation between him and Mr. Bingley, who came from the dance for a few
minutes to press his friend to join it.
“Come, Darcy,” said he, “I must have you dance. I hate to see you standing about by
yourself in this stupid manner. You had much better dance.”
“I certainly shall not. You know how I detest it, unless I am particularly acquainted
with my partner. At such an assembly as this, it would be insupportable. Your sisters
are engaged, and there is not another woman in the room whom it would not be a
punishment to me to stand up with.”
“I would not be so fastidious as you are,” cried Bingley, “for a kingdom! Upon my
honour, I never met with so many pleasant girls in my life as I have this evening; and
there are several of them, you see, uncommonly pretty.”
“You are dancing with the only handsome girl in the room,” said Mr. Darcy, looking at
the eldest Miss Bennet.
“Oh, she is the most beautiful creature I ever beheld! But there is one of her sisters
sitting down just behind you, who is very pretty, and I dare say very agreeable. Do let
me ask my partner to introduce you.”
“Which do you mean?” and turning round, he looked for a moment at Elizabeth, till,
catching her eye, he withdrew his own, and coldly said, “She is tolerable: but not
handsome enough to tempt me; and I am in no humour at present to give consequence to
young ladies who are slighted by other men. You had better return to your partner and
enjoy her smiles, for you are wasting your time with me.”
Mr. Bingley followed his advice. Mr. Darcy walked off; and Elizabeth remained with no
very cordial feelings towards him. She told the story, however, with great spirit among
her friends; for she had a lively, playful disposition, which delighted in anything
ridiculous.

stem.text: The Bennet daughters did not meet Mr Bingley when he called at their house. Read lines 5 to 8. What were they able to find out about him?

rows.key: What colour his coat was, and what colour his horse was.

options.value: That he was cheerful and talked to everybody.
options.tagChildHint: A true fact from somewhere else does not answer this question. Find the part the question points to.
options.execution: Being cheerful and talking to everybody is Mr Bingley at lines 36 and 37, at the ball — true, and a different part of the passage. In the window, line 8 answers the stem: 'window, that he wore a blue coat and rode'.

options.value: That he had ten thousand pounds a year.
options.tagChildHint: Two people are being described. Check which one each detail belongs to.
options.execution: Ten thousand a year is Mr Darcy's, at line 29, carried across to Mr Bingley. In the window, line 8 answers the stem: 'window, that he wore a blue coat and rode'.

options.value: What colour his coat was, and what colour his horse was.
That he stayed about ten minutes with their father.
options.tagChildHint: Being in the lines is not enough. Check it answers the question you were asked.
options.execution: Line 5 does say he sat about ten minutes. True, inside the window, and it is what MR BENNET got out of the visit rather than what the daughters found out.

options.value: That he liked the big house he had taken.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: Nothing says he liked the house; taking it makes it sound like something they could have learned.

rows.hintCore: What could you see from a window, and no more than that?
rows.walkScript: Go to the upper window, line 8. He 'wore a blue coat and rode a black horse'. So the colours are all they found out. His money and manners come later.

stem.text: Mr Bingley hoped for something on this visit that he did not get. Read lines 5 to 6. What was it?

rows.key: A look at Mr Bennet's daughters.

options.value: A book from Mr Bennet's library.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: The library is line 5 and true, and no book is mentioned anywhere in the passage.

options.value: A look at Mr Bennet's daughters.
A chance to invite the Bennets to dinner at his own house.
options.tagChildHint: Ask who is doing it and who it is being done to.
options.execution: It reverses who invites whom: line 9 has the invitation going FROM the Bennets.

options.value: A ride on Mr Bennet's black horse.
options.tagChildHint: Two people are being described. Check which one each detail belongs to.
options.execution: The black horse at line 8 is a thing the ladies saw, turned into something he wanted. In the window, line 5 answers the stem: 'him in his library. He had entertained hopes of'.

options.value: A dance with the eldest Miss Bennet.
options.tagChildHint: A true fact from somewhere else does not answer this question. Find the part the question points to.
options.execution: The dancing is lines 36 to 41, at the assembly, weeks after this visit. In the window, line 5 answers the stem: 'him in his library. He had entertained hopes of'.

rows.hintCore: Who did he want to see, and who did he actually see?
rows.walkScript: Turn to lines 5 and 6. He hoped to see the young ladies, but 'saw only the father'. So he missed a look at the daughters. The dance comes much later.

stem.text: Mr Bingley said no to the Bennets' dinner. Read lines 9 to 12. What reason did his answer give?

rows.key: He had to be in London the next day.

options.value: He had promised to dine with Lady Lucas instead.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: Lady Lucas is at line 15 and says nothing about dining; the answer names no rival engagement at all.

options.value: He did not want to meet the Bennet daughters.
options.tagChildHint: A reason has to be given, not guessed. Ask what the text says about why.
options.execution: A wish to avoid the daughters is supplied; lines 5 and 6 have him hoping to see them.

options.value: He was busy planning the courses for a dinner of his own.
options.tagChildHint: Two people are being described. Check which one each detail belongs to.
options.execution: The planning of courses at lines 9 and 10 is MRS BENNET'S, carried across to him.

options.value: He had to be in London the next day.
He had gone to London to gather a big group for the ball.
options.tagChildHint: A true fact from somewhere else does not answer this question. Find the part the question points to.
options.execution: The London party is Lady Lucas's guess at lines 15 to 17, after the refusal and not part of it. In the window, line 11 answers the stem: 'which deferred it all. Mr. Bingley was obliged to'.

rows.hintCore: Find the words 'obliged to be in town'.
rows.walkScript: Look at lines 11 and 12. His answer says he was obliged to be in town the following day. 'Town' means London here. He simply had to be somewhere else.

stem.text: Mr Bingley's answer upset Mrs Bennet. Read lines 13 to 16. What was she most afraid of?

rows.key: That he would keep moving about and never really live at Netherfield.

options.value: That he would keep moving about and never really live at Netherfield.
That her dinner had all been cooked and would now be wasted.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: Nothing says the dinner was cooked; line 10 has her planning courses and the answer arriving before it happened.

options.value: That he had gone to London to look for guests for the ball.
options.tagChildHint: Two people are being described. Check which one each detail belongs to.
options.execution: The guest-gathering at lines 16 and 17 is Lady Lucas's comfort, and this transfers it into Mrs Bennet's fear.

options.value: That the girls would have to meet twelve strange ladies.
options.tagChildHint: A true fact from somewhere else does not answer this question. Find the part the question points to.
options.execution: The twelve ladies are line 18, and it is the GIRLS who grieve over them at line 18, not Mrs Bennet. In the window, line 14 answers the stem: 'his arrival in Hertfordshire; and she began to fear'.

options.value: That Mr Bingley did not like her daughters.
options.tagChildHint: A reason has to be given, not guessed. Ask what the text says about why.
options.execution: A dislike of her daughters is supplied; the passage gives his reason as business in town.

rows.hintCore: Find the words 'she began to fear' and read what comes next.
rows.walkScript: Line 14 says 'she began to fear'. He might be 'flying about from one place to another'. So she fears he will never settle. The dinner comes earlier, the guests later.

stem.text: Read lines 17 to 21. Line 21 says: 'when the party entered the assembly-room'. What does 'party' mean here?

rows.key: A group of people who arrive together.

options.value: A celebration with food, music and games.
options.tagChildHint: You know one meaning for this word. Check that meaning fits what the sentence is saying here.
options.execution: A birthday party is the sense a child meets first, and the word sits in a sentence about a ball.

options.value: The ball that Mr Bingley talked of giving at Netherfield.
options.tagChildHint: A true fact from somewhere else does not answer this question. Find the part the question points to.
options.execution: The Netherfield ball is line 38, at the very end of the evening — a true event from a different part. In the window, line 21 answers the stem: 'cousin. And when the party entered the assembly-room, it'.

options.value: A group of people who arrive together.
A group of people who run a country together.
options.tagChildHint: More than one meaning fits this word. Find the words nearby that decide which one it has to be.
options.execution: The political sense is a real second sense of the word and nothing in the line supports it.

options.value: Everybody who came to the assembly that night.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: Everybody at the assembly is not stated as a party; line 21 counts the party as five.

rows.hintCore: Can a birthday party walk into a room?
rows.walkScript: Read line 21 to the full stop. The party 'entered' the room, and five people are named. So a party here is a group who come in together. The ball comes later.

stem.text: Read lines 17 to 23. Who actually came into the assembly-room with Mr Bingley?

rows.key: His two sisters, the husband of the elder sister, and one other young man.

options.value: His five sisters and a cousin.
options.tagChildHint: Being in the lines is not enough. Check it answers the question you were asked.
options.execution: Five sisters and a cousin is line 20, the SECOND report. True, inside the window, and the wrong element for a question about who actually walked in.

options.value: Twelve ladies and seven gentlemen.
options.tagChildHint: Check what happened first, and what the question asks for.
options.execution: Twelve ladies and seven gentlemen is the FIRST report at lines 17 and 18, superseded twice before line 21. An early stage of the news is taken as the final state.

options.value: His two sisters, Mr Hurst and Mr Bennet.
options.tagChildHint: Two answers can look almost the same. Find what differs and check it against the text.
options.execution: One name changed: Mr Bennet for the young man. Everything else matches line 22.

options.value: His two sisters and both their husbands.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: Only one husband is named — 'the husband of the eldest' at line 22 — and a second is supplied.

options.value: His two sisters, the husband of the elder sister, and one other young man.

rows.hintCore: Which sentence tells you who really walked in?
rows.walkScript: Lines 21 to 23 name them. The group was 'only five altogether'. Take Mr Bingley out: two sisters, a husband, a young man. The bigger numbers come earlier.

stem.text: First the village hears of twelve ladies and seven gentlemen. Then it hears six. Then only five people arrive. Read lines 17 to 23. Why does the writer give us all three numbers?

rows.key: To show how much the village talk changed each time it was passed on.

options.value: To show that Mr Bingley kept changing his mind about who to bring.
options.tagChildHint: Ask what exactly made this happen. Re-read the moment step by step.
options.execution: The changing is put on Mr Bingley; the numbers change in the village's mouth at lines 17 to 21 and he is never asked.

options.value: To show how much the village talk changed each time it was passed on.
To show that the girls were looking forward to meeting new people.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: Line 18 has the girls GRIEVING over the number of ladies, which is the opposite of looking forward.

options.value: To show that Mr Bingley really did have five sisters.
options.tagChildHint: Being in the lines is not enough. Check it answers the question you were asked.
options.execution: The five sisters are line 20, inside the window, and part of the report line 21 corrects rather than a reason for giving three numbers.

options.value: To make sure the reader counts the guests carefully.
options.tagChildHint: Writers repeat on purpose. Ask what the echo does to the reader.
options.execution: The three numbers are read as an instruction to the reader rather than as talk changing shape.

rows.hintCore: Who was doing the talking each time a number changed?
rows.walkScript: Start at line 17 with the numbers. First 'a report' of twelve, then six, then five walk in. So the number shrinks as the news passes on. Mr Bingley never gave one.

stem.text: Read lines 24 to 34. Line 24 uses 'countenance' about Mr Bingley and line 34 about Mr Darcy. What does it mean both times?

rows.key: A person's face, and the look on it.

options.value: A person's face, and the look on it.
The way a person speaks to other people.
options.tagChildHint: Being in the lines is not enough. Check it answers the question you were asked.
options.execution: The way a person speaks is lines 24 and 25 — 'easy, unaffected manners'. True, inside the window, and a different quality from the one the word names.

options.value: Letting something happen, or agreeing to it.
options.tagChildHint: More than one meaning fits this word. Find the words nearby that decide which one it has to be.
options.execution: To countenance something is a real second sense of the word, and nothing in either line is about permission.

options.value: The good name a person's family has in the county.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: A family's good name is not in the passage; 'countenance' sounds like it should be.

options.value: A count of how many people are in a room.
options.tagChildHint: Two answers can look almost the same. Find what differs and check it against the text.
options.execution: 'Countenance' is skimmed for the word 'count' inside it.

rows.hintCore: One man's is pleasant and the other's is forbidding. Which part of a person?
rows.walkScript: Put lines 24 and 34 side by side. One countenance is 'pleasant', the other 'forbidding'. So it means a face, and its look. Agreeing and counting are other senses.

stem.text: When Mr Darcy first walked in, the room thought very well of him. Read lines 26 to 30. Why?

rows.key: Because of his looks, and because of the news that he was very rich.

options.value: Because he danced with lots of different ladies.
options.tagChildHint: Two people are being described. Check which one each detail belongs to.
options.execution: Dancing every dance is Mr Bingley at line 37, carried across to Mr Darcy, who dances twice. In the window, line 27 answers the stem: 'drew the attention of the room by his fine'.

options.value: Because he spoke kindly to everyone he was introduced to.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: Speaking kindly is nowhere; line 40 has him decline being introduced to anyone.

options.value: Because he was the tallest man in the room.
options.tagChildHint: Does the passage really go that far? Check the strongest word in the option.
options.execution: 'The tallest man in the room' is the absolute version of line 27's 'fine, tall person'.

options.value: Because of his looks, and because of the news that he was very rich.
Because he owned a large estate in Derbyshire.
options.tagChildHint: A true fact from somewhere else does not answer this question. Find the part the question points to.
options.execution: The Derbyshire estate is line 33, and it appears only when the room has turned against him. In the window, line 27 answers the stem: 'drew the attention of the room by his fine'.

rows.hintCore: What had everybody heard about him within five minutes?
rows.walkScript: Start at line 27, with 'his fine, tall person'. Line 29 adds 'ten thousand a year'. So his looks and his money won the room. The estate is named later.

stem.text: Halfway through the evening, people changed their minds about Mr Darcy. Read lines 30 to 35. What changed them?

rows.key: The way he behaved, as if he were better than everyone there.

options.value: They found out that he was not really rich after all.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: Nothing says the money was doubted; line 33 still calls the estate large.

options.value: They decided he was less good-looking than Mr Bingley.
options.tagChildHint: Ask who is doing it and who it is being done to.
options.execution: It reverses line 30, where the ladies declare him HANDSOMER than Mr Bingley.

options.value: The way he behaved, as if he were better than everyone there.
He complained that the ball had ended too early.
options.tagChildHint: Two people are being described. Check which one each detail belongs to.
options.execution: Complaining that the ball closed early is Mr Bingley at line 37, transferred to Mr Darcy. In the window, line 31 answers the stem: 'with great admiration for about half the evening, till'.

options.value: Everybody disliked him from the moment he walked in.
options.tagChildHint: Does the passage really go that far? Check the strongest word in the option.
options.execution: 'From the moment he walked in' overstates: line 30 has him admired for half the evening.

rows.hintCore: Find the word 'till' in line 31 and read on from there.
rows.walkScript: Find 'till' in line 31. 'His manners gave a disgust' and turned the tide. So his behaviour changed the room's mind. His money and looks come earlier.

stem.text: Read lines 36 to 41. The writer suddenly says: 'What a contrast between him and his friend!' Why is that sentence put there?

quotes.text: What a contrast between him and his friend!

rows.key: To make the reader notice how differently the two men were behaving.

options.value: To tell the reader that the two men had fallen out.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: A quarrel is nowhere in the passage; the two are together again at lines 49 and 51.

options.value: To show that Mr Bingley was cross about something.
options.tagChildHint: Being in the lines is not enough. Check it answers the question you were asked.
options.execution: The anger at line 37 is inside the window and is Mr Bingley's, about the ball closing early — the wrong element of a line the item does use.

options.value: To show that the writer likes Mr Darcy the better of the two.
options.tagChildHint: A reason has to be given, not guessed. Ask what the text says about why.
options.execution: A preference is supplied for the writer, who states the contrast and takes no side in it.

options.value: To make the reader notice how differently the two men were behaving.
To show that the two men were really rather alike.
options.tagChildHint: Some words tell you how two things go together. Find that word and read it again.
options.execution: 'Contrast' is read as its opposite. The sentence says the two men are unlike, and this answers that they are alike.

rows.hintCore: Read the sentence before it and the sentence after it.
rows.walkScript: Look at each side, lines 36 to 41. Mr Bingley 'danced every dance'; Mr Darcy walks about alone. So you see how differently they behave. Nothing says they fell out.

stem.text: Read lines 39 to 41. How many dances did Mr Darcy dance, and who did he dance with?

rows.key: Two: one with Mrs Hurst and one with Miss Bingley.

options.value: Every dance of the evening.
options.tagChildHint: Two people are being described. Check which one each detail belongs to.
options.execution: Every dance is Mr Bingley's at line 37, one line above, carried across to Mr Darcy. In the window, line 39 answers the stem: 'speak for themselves. What a contrast between him and'.

options.value: Two: one with Mrs Hurst and one with Miss Bingley.
Two: one with Miss Bingley and one with Elizabeth.
options.tagChildHint: Two answers can look almost the same. Find what differs and check it against the text.
options.execution: One name changed: Elizabeth for Mrs Hurst. The count and the shape of line 40 are kept.

options.value: None at all.
options.tagChildHint: Does the passage really go that far? Check the strongest word in the option.
options.execution: 'None at all' is the absolute version of 'danced only once... and once' at lines 39 and 40.

options.value: Three: with Mrs Hurst, Miss Bingley and Miss Bennet.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: A third dance with Miss Bennet is supplied; she dances with Mr Bingley at line 63 and never with him.

rows.hintCore: Count how many times the word 'once' appears.
rows.walkScript: The sentence about Mr Darcy starts at line 39. He danced once with Mrs Hurst and once with Miss Bingley. That is two dances, and every dance belongs to Mr Bingley.

stem.text: Read lines 41 to 43. The writer says: 'His character was decided. He was the proudest, most disagreeable man in the world.' What do these short, sure sentences do?

quotes.text: His character was decided. He was the proudest, most disagreeable man in the world

rows.key: They make the room's quick opinion sound like a settled fact.

options.value: They prove that Mr Darcy really was the worst man alive.
options.tagChildHint: Does the passage really go that far? Check the strongest word in the option.
options.execution: 'Really was the worst man alive' takes the room's verdict as the writer's own finding.

options.value: They show that the writer had run out of things to say about him.
options.tagChildHint: A reason has to be given, not guessed. Ask what the text says about why.
options.execution: A motive is supplied for the writer; the shortness is doing the room's certainty, not his.

options.value: They make the room's quick opinion sound like a settled fact.
They show that Mr Darcy had at last made up his mind about something.
options.tagChildHint: You know one meaning for this word. Check that meaning fits what the sentence is saying here.
options.execution: Takes 'his character was decided' as Mr Darcy deciding something. NOTE REPAIRED 2026-08-16 (delivery 52): 'decided' meaning MADE A DECISION is the sense that arrives first, not 'the other sense' — the passage's sense, settled and no longer open to question, is the rarer one. The error is a dominant sense displacing a rarer one. Tag grandfathered; the note is not.

options.value: They tell us that Mr Darcy said nothing to anybody all evening.
options.tagChildHint: A true fact from somewhere else does not answer this question. Find the part the question points to.
options.execution: Line 41 has him 'speaking occasionally to one of his own party', so he does speak.

rows.hintCore: Whose opinion is this — the writer's own, or the room's?
rows.walkScript: Look at line 42: 'His character was decided'. Nobody is named as deciding it. So the room's hasty view sounds like a fact. It comes after one night.

stem.text: Mrs Bennet disliked Mr Darcy more strongly than anybody else in the room did. Read lines 44 to 46. What made her feeling so strong?

rows.key: He had been rude about one of her daughters.

options.value: He had been rude about one of her daughters.
He would not let anyone introduce him to her.
options.tagChildHint: A true fact from somewhere else does not answer this question. Find the part the question points to.
options.execution: Declining to be introduced is line 40, and it is to any other LADY, not to Mrs Bennet in particular. In the window, line 44 answers the stem: 'Amongst the most violent against him was Mrs. Bennet'.

options.value: He had told Mr Bennet that he did not like the neighbourhood.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: Mr Bennet is not at the ball at all in this passage, and no such remark is made.

options.value: Mr Bingley had chosen to dance with her eldest daughter.
options.tagChildHint: Ask what exactly made this happen. Re-read the moment step by step.
options.execution: The cause is moved to Mr Bingley's dancing at line 63; lines 45 and 46 name the slight as the reason.

options.value: He was the proudest man in the world, and she hated proud people.
options.tagChildHint: Does the passage really go that far? Check the strongest word in the option.
options.execution: 'The proudest man in the world' at line 42 is offered as her reason, which makes her feeling general when lines 45 and 46 make it particular.

rows.hintCore: The words 'one of her daughters' are the clue. Why do they matter to her?
rows.walkScript: Read lines 44 to 46. He had 'slighted one of her daughters'. Slighted means treated as nothing. So the sting is her own child.

stem.text: Elizabeth had to sit down for two dances. Read lines 47 to 48. Why?

rows.key: There were not enough gentlemen for all the ladies.

options.value: She did not feel like dancing that evening.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: A wish not to dance is supplied; line 47 says she was OBLIGED to sit down.

options.value: Mr Darcy had refused to dance with her.
options.tagChildHint: Ask what exactly made this happen. Re-read the moment step by step.
options.execution: Mr Darcy's refusal is lines 66 and 67 and comes after she is already sitting; the cause and the effect are swapped.

options.value: She wanted to listen to Mr Darcy and Mr Bingley talking.
options.tagChildHint: A reason has to be given, not guessed. Ask what the text says about why.
options.execution: A motive is supplied; line 48 has the overhearing happen because he stood near enough, not because she arranged it.

options.value: There were not enough gentlemen for all the ladies.
Her eldest sister was dancing with Mr Bingley.
options.tagChildHint: A true fact from somewhere else does not answer this question. Find the part the question points to.
options.execution: Her eldest sister dancing with Mr Bingley is line 60, true, and not the reason line 47 gives.

rows.hintCore: What does 'scarcity of gentlemen' mean?
rows.walkScript: Line 47 holds the reason. She was 'obliged, by the scarcity of gentlemen, to sit down'. A scarcity means too few men for the ladies. Mr Darcy's words come later.

stem.text: Elizabeth hears Mr Darcy's words herself. A friend does not tell her later. Read lines 47 to 50. Why is that a good choice?

rows.key: The reader hears the unkind words at the very moment Elizabeth does.

options.value: It shows that Elizabeth enjoyed listening in on other people.
options.tagChildHint: A reason has to be given, not guessed. Ask what the text says about why.
options.execution: A taste for listening in is supplied; line 48 has him standing near enough for her to overhear.

options.value: It shows that the room had almost emptied by then.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: An empty room is not stated; line 49 has Mr Bingley coming from the dance, so it is in progress.

options.value: The reader hears the unkind words at the very moment Elizabeth does.
Mr Bingley had planned for her to hear his kind words about her.
options.tagChildHint: Ask what exactly made this happen. Re-read the moment step by step.
options.execution: The planning is given to Mr Bingley, and the words Elizabeth hears are Mr Darcy's, not his.

options.value: It shows that Mr Darcy was speaking loudly to the whole room.
options.tagChildHint: Some options only copy words from the passage. Ask what those words are telling you.
options.execution: 'Near enough for her to overhear' at line 48 is read as loudly enough for the room.

rows.hintCore: Do you hear the words, or only hear about them later?
rows.walkScript: Line 48 puts him 'near enough for her to overhear'. So the words come in his voice. You hear them as Elizabeth does. The room hears nothing of this.

stem.text: Read lines 51 and 52. Mr Bingley says to his friend: 'I hate to see you standing about by yourself in this stupid manner.' What is Mr Bingley trying to do?

quotes.text: I hate to see you standing about by yourself in this stupid manner

rows.key: Get his friend to join the dancing.

options.value: Tell his friend off for being rude about the ladies.
options.tagChildHint: A true fact from somewhere else does not answer this question. Find the part the question points to.
options.execution: The rudeness about the ladies is lines 55 and 56, in Mr Darcy's reply, after this speech. In the window, line 51 answers the stem: '“Come, Darcy,” said he, “I must have you dance'.

options.value: Get his friend to join the dancing.
Ask his friend to leave the ball and go home.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: Going home is nowhere; the speech asks him to move onto the floor, not off it.

options.value: Make his friend feel sorry for the ladies who have no partner.
options.tagChildHint: A reason has to be given, not guessed. Ask what the text says about why.
options.execution: Pity for partnerless ladies is supplied; the speech is about his friend and no one else.

rows.hintCore: What does he ask for at the start, and again at the end?
rows.walkScript: Read the speech, lines 51 and 52. It opens 'I must have you dance', ends 'You had much better dance'. So he wants his friend dancing. 'Stupid' describes the standing about.

stem.text: Read lines 53 to 56. Mr Darcy says: 'Your sisters are engaged.' What does 'engaged' mean here?

rows.key: They have already promised their dances to other partners.

options.value: They have promised to marry somebody.
options.tagChildHint: You know one meaning for this word. Check that meaning fits what the sentence is saying here.
options.execution: Promised in marriage is the sense a child meets first, and a ballroom full of unmarried people supports it.

options.value: They are busy and cannot be spoken to.
options.tagChildHint: More than one meaning fits this word. Find the words nearby that decide which one it has to be.
options.execution: Busy and not to be interrupted sits right beside the passage sense and is not it: line 54 is about who is free to DANCE.

options.value: They are standing and talking with Mr Bingley.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: Standing and talking with Mr Bingley is not stated; he is dancing at line 60.

options.value: They do not want to dance with Mr Darcy.
options.tagChildHint: A reason has to be given, not guessed. Ask what the text says about why.
options.execution: A wish not to dance with him is supplied; line 54 says nothing about what the sisters want.

options.value: They have already promised their dances to other partners.

rows.hintCore: He is making a list of who is free to dance. Where do the sisters go on that list?
rows.walkScript: Look at the speech, lines 53 to 56. He lists who he might dance with, crossing the sisters off. So their dances are already promised. Marriage is the better-known sense.

stem.text: Read lines 57 to 59. Mr Bingley cries: 'I would not be so fastidious as you are.' What does 'fastidious' mean here?

quotes.text: I would not be so fastidious as you are

rows.key: Very hard to please.

options.value: Very hard to please.
Very quick and in a hurry.
options.tagChildHint: Two answers can look almost the same. Find what differs and check it against the text.
options.execution: 'Fastidious' is skimmed as though it were 'fast'.

options.value: Very shy with people you do not know.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: Shyness is not in the passage; Mr Darcy's objection at lines 53 and 54 is to the company, not to himself.

options.value: Very tidy and neat.
options.tagChildHint: More than one meaning fits this word. Find the words nearby that decide which one it has to be.
options.execution: Tidy and neat is a real everyday use of the word and nothing in these lines is about order.

options.value: Very rude to other people.
options.tagChildHint: Pick the word you can prove from the text. Close is not the same.
options.execution: Rudeness is an approximation: Mr Darcy IS rude at line 66, and that is not what 'fastidious' names.

rows.hintCore: The two friends are looking at the very same room. How are they different about it?
rows.walkScript: Lines 57 to 59 give the sense. Bingley met many 'pleasant girls'; Darcy sees none worth a dance. So fastidious means very hard to please. Shy and tidy do not fit here.

stem.text: Read lines 65 to 67. Mr Darcy says Elizabeth 'is tolerable: but not handsome enough to tempt me'. What does 'tolerable' mean here?

rows.key: Only just good enough to look at.

options.value: Kind, and easy to get along with.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: Kindness is nowhere in the sentence; 'tolerable' sounds like a word about temperament.

options.value: Good at putting up with things without complaining.
options.tagChildHint: The parts of a word do not always add up. Check the whole word in the sentence.
options.execution: The target is TOLERABLE. 'Putting up with things without complaining' is the meaning of TOLERANT, a different word the target resembles in form; the line is about how she looks. NOTE REPAIRED 2026-08-16 (delivery 52): this was described as 'a real second sense of the word' and it is not a sense of the target at all. Tag grandfathered under the era exception; a note that is wrong about English is not.

options.value: Only just good enough to look at.
Very good-looking, so he is paying her a compliment.
options.tagChildHint: Pick the word you can prove from the text. Close is not the same.
options.execution: Reads the word as praise, which line 66's 'but not handsome enough' immediately cancels.

options.value: Too proud to dance with anybody.
options.tagChildHint: Ask who is doing it and who it is being done to.
options.execution: Turns the word back on Mr Darcy: it describes Elizabeth, and the pride is his.

rows.hintCore: Read the word 'but' that follows. It takes the praise straight back.
rows.walkScript: Read on from 'tolerable' in line 66. It is 'but not handsome enough to tempt me'. So it means only just good enough. Putting up with things is the other sense.

stem.text: Read lines 70 to 73. Elizabeth 'told the story, however, with great spirit'. What does 'spirit' mean here?

rows.key: Being lively and cheerful.

options.value: A ghost.
options.tagChildHint: You know one meaning for this word. Check that meaning fits what the sentence is saying here.
options.execution: A ghost is the sense a child meets first, and nothing in the sentence rules it out until you read on.

options.value: Anger.
options.tagChildHint: Pick the word you can prove from the text. Close is not the same.
options.execution: Anger is an approximation of the feeling: line 70 gives 'no very cordial feelings', and line 71 gives the telling as lively.

options.value: Care and quietness, so that nobody else heard.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: Quietness is not stated; line 71 has her telling it 'among her friends'.

options.value: Being lively and cheerful.
Bravery when you are in danger.
options.tagChildHint: More than one meaning fits this word. Find the words nearby that decide which one it has to be.
options.execution: Bravery in danger is a real second sense of 'spirit' and there is no danger in the line.

rows.hintCore: Read on past 'spirit'. The rest of the sentence tells you what she was like.
rows.walkScript: Line 71 does not stop at 'spirit'. Read on to line 72: she had 'a lively, playful disposition'. So spirit here means lively and cheerful. A ghost is the other sense.

stem.text: At the end, Elizabeth turns what happened into a story for her friends. Read lines 70 to 73. What does this tell us about her?

rows.key: She can find the funny side of things, even when she has been treated badly.

options.value: She has completely forgiven Mr Darcy.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: Forgiveness is not stated; line 70 leaves her with 'no very cordial feelings towards him'.

options.value: She can find the funny side of things, even when she has been treated badly.
She wants her friends to feel sorry for her.
options.tagChildHint: A reason has to be given, not guessed. Ask what the text says about why.
options.execution: A wish for sympathy is supplied; lines 71 and 72 give her a lively, playful disposition instead.

options.value: What Mr Darcy said did not bother her at all.
options.tagChildHint: Does the passage really go that far? Check the strongest word in the option.
options.execution: 'Did not bother her at all' overstates: line 70 says her feelings towards him were not cordial.

options.value: She thinks Mr Darcy is a fine, handsome man.
options.tagChildHint: A true fact from somewhere else does not answer this question. Find the part the question points to.
options.execution: The praise of his looks is line 30, from the ladies of the room, and it is withdrawn by line 34. In the window, line 70 answers the stem: 'Mr. Bingley followed his advice. Mr. Darcy walked off'.

rows.hintCore: She feels two things at once here. What are they?
rows.walkScript: Lines 70 to 73 hold two things. She has 'no very cordial feelings', yet tells it 'with great spirit'. So she finds the funny side. The handsome praise comes earlier.

stem.text: Think about the whole passage. How do we learn what the people in it are like?

rows.key: We are told what others say of them, but never whether the writer agrees.

options.value: We are told what the writer thinks, and not only what the room says.
options.tagChildHint: Before you take this as true, ask whose opinion it is.
options.execution: Reads the reported verdicts as the writer's own. Line 42's 'His character was decided' names nobody as deciding it, which is the point this option misses.

options.value: We are shown what they do, but never told whether the writer approves.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: The showing is there — line 37 has Mr Bingley dancing every dance — but line 38 answers it with 'such amiable qualities must speak for themselves', which declines the plain telling this half-claims.

options.value: We are given only Elizabeth's view, and no other opinion is ever allowed.
options.tagChildHint: Does the passage really go that far? Check the strongest word in the option.
options.execution: Elizabeth does not appear until line 47 and gives no verdict at all; the opinions at lines 29, 42 and 44 belong to the room and to Mrs Bennet.

options.value: We are told what others say of them, but never whether the writer agrees.

rows.hintCore: You are about to say what the writer thinks of them. Find the line where he says it.
rows.walkScript: Line 29 has the gentlemen and the ladies pronouncing. Line 42 says his character was decided, and names nobody. Line 44 gives Mrs Bennet's dislike. Each verdict belongs to somebody in the room.
